g.text: against two amateurs, the Duke of Brunswick and Count Isouard. It
has become the standard example of what quick development does to an
opponent who spends moves on other things.
Watch how every white move brings a new piece into play, while Black
twice moves pieces that are already out.
Count the developed pieces after move 12: White has everything in
play and the king is safe. Black's king is still in the centre, the
h8-rook has never moved, and the bishop on f8 has not seen the game.
a b c d e f g h
Before castling, the squares next to the king are protected by the
king alone. The f7 square for Black, and f2 for White, are the
classic targets. This trap is named after L
